item.title: [MLB.com] Padres get revenge with commanding sweep of Cubs in Wild Card Series
item.dc:creator: AJ Cassavell

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO -- The Padres spent September as the hottest team in baseball, surging into the postseason and securing a Wild Card Series at Petco Park.
All summer, Sheets had been playing through a nasty injury -- a plantar plate tear in his left foot. He wondered if he’d be able to contribute at all. There was certainly no way he could contribute defensively.
But maybe … just maybe … if Sheets could heal just enough … he could deliver a meaningful swing or two in the postseason.
A swing like this one.
Sheets came off the bench to deliver the swing that broke the Cubs in Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series on Wednesday night -- a pinch-hit, two-run home run that sent Petco Park into delirium and the Padres on course for Milwaukee.
With their 4-1 victory over the Cubs, San Diego secured a trip to the NL Division Series against the Brewers, beginning on Saturday night. But first, the Padres staged a party in the home clubhouse at Petco Park.
Before the champagne was popped and the cigars were lit, manager Craig Stammen stood at the center of it all.
“We had 13 bricks to lay,” Stammen said. “Two down, 11 more to go.”
The next three almost certainly won’t come quite so easily. For the fourth time in seven seasons, the Padres are headed to the NLDS, where they’ll meet Milwaukee in a playoff series for the first time. The Brewers own the sport’s best record. Jacob Misiorowski, the presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner, takes the ball first.
“We know who they’re throwing Game 1,” said Xander Bogaerts. “So let’s celebrate today. And then be ready for that fastball.”
Call it sweet revenge for the Padres after their 2025 season came to an end with a Wild Card Series exit at Wrigley Field.
They made quick work of the Cubs, dispatching them in two games that were never all that close. The two teams played 18 innings at Petco Park this week. The Padres led after 17 of them. The Chicago offense, which scored more runs than any other team during the regular season, was held to one across two playoff games.
“We just didn't play well enough,” said Cubs manager Craig Counsell. “And they're playing really well.”
In Game 1, the Padres were a force of nature. The ballpark partied from the very first pitch (a Michael King fastball past Pete Crow-Armstrong) to the very last pitch (Joe Musgrove punctuating his triumphant return to the mound with a game-ending strikeout). They won, 8-0.
“I’ve never seen anything like it,” Manny Machado, a veteran of eight postseasons, said of the home crowd this week. “That was huge.”
Game 2 brought a different kind of postseason energy. A party, to be sure. But one with some tension mixed in. October baseball, on the final day of September.
San Diego jumped in front in the second with Bogaerts’ RBI single and Ethan Salas’ sacrifice fly. (Salas, the youngest player in history to catch a postseason game, also became the youngest player at any position with a postseason sac fly -- since at least 1954 when that stat was fully tracked.)
But the Cubs scratched a run back against Nick Pivetta in the fourth and worked their way into the Padres’ bullpen. Crow-Armstrong and the top of the lineup loomed in the fifth.
There were two outs and a runner aboard, and Counsell had gone with right-hander Daniel Palencia. Sheets strode to the on-deck circle, then, eventually, the batter’s box -- with those three familiar thuds echoing through the Petco Park sound system.
HO-LY SHEETS.
“You just get ready for that moment, so when it happens you don’t feel like it’s sped up on you,” Sheets said. “To see this fanbase the whole entire time, I just wanted to get in front of them, I wanted to play. These guys brought it.”
This was the moment the Padres had been planning for. When Sheets is right, he mashes right-handed pitching. He’s a weapon in the clutch and can be a force off the bench.
“We had talked about that move, probably more than I care to admit in my office, with our pro scouting and advanced scouting,” Stammen said. “We felt like Gavin was a good matchup for some of their right-handed pitching. … That’s why we put him on the bench today, just in case he could pop one like that in a big situation.
“Doesn’t always work out that way. But he made us all look good.”
In the end, Sheets would take all of one swing across two games in the series. He made it count.
Palencia threw a 100.8 mph fastball at the bottom of the zone on the inner half. Sheets turned on it -- the hardest pitch any Padre has ever homered on, regular or postseason.
“That’s Dairy Bonds, baby,” said Jackson Merrill, between puffs of a cigar in a raucous Padres clubhouse. “That’s what he does -- 101, down and in. You just don’t see that. That was sick. That was one of the cooler home runs I’ve ever seen.”
And then get ready for that fastball.

item.title: [MLB.com] Phillies vs. Braves NL Wild Card Series Game 3 FAQ (8 ET, NBC/Peacock)
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman; Todd Zolecki; Paul Casella
item.description: In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023. “Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a lit
item.content:encoded:
In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023.
“Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a little bit, it's the same as we did [after Game 1]: Turn the page, and move on to tomorrow and show up ready to do the same thing.”
So, what could the Phillies and Braves possibly have in store for their winner-take-all showdown?
While that’s the biggest question looming over the National League Wild Card Series, it’s far from the only one. Here’s everything you need to know about Game 3:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
The game will begin at 8 p.m. ET and air on NBC and Peacock.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Phillies: TBD
The Phillies planned to meet following Game 2 to discuss their pitching plans for this week’s third elimination game. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said Monday that Aaron Nola was setting up to start Game 3, but there’s no question things can change. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see ace Zack Wheeler start on short rest. If he doesn’t start, there’s no doubt he’d enter the game in relief.
Braves: TBD
Grant Holmes will attempt to handle the bulk of the innings. But the Braves haven’t said whether he’ll start or possibly follow an opener. The top options to open are left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter. Either would be tasked with handling Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber in the first inning.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Braves: The Braves’ lineup appears much more formidable against right-handed pitchers. With Mike Yastrzemski in left field, Mauricio Dubón would move to shortstop, which was where Ha-Seong Kim started during the first two games.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Phillies: Mattingly said it’s “all hands on deck,” although closer Jhoan Duran wasn’t available in Game 2. Mattingly said he hoped he’d have Duran in Game 3. But other than Cristopher Sánchez, who started Game 2, probably every pitcher on the Phillies’ staff will be available in some capacity in Game 3. That’s everybody from Wheeler to Luzardo to Painter.
Braves: Closer Raisel Iglesias and his top setup men Didier Fuentes and Dylan Lee both pitched in the first two games of this series. Each should be available in this winner-take-all game. Robert Suarez hasn’t been utilized yet. He missed three months with an elbow ailment before making two appearances last week. But manager Walt Weiss may have no other choice but to turn to the right-hander, who posted a 0.56 ERA in 31 appearances before his elbow became a problem in June.
Any injuries of note?
Braves: OF Lane Thomas could be available during the NLDS. Starting pitchers Bryce Elder (arthroscopic knee surgery), Reynaldo López (right shoulder inflammation) and Martín Pérez (lower back discomfort) may also be available in future rounds.
Who is hot and who is not?
Phillies: Home runs often come in bunches for Schwarber and Harper. Did their back-to-back homers in the eighth inning in Game 2 get them going? Bohm is 3-for-8 with one double and one home run in the series. After struggling all season, Realmuto has two hits and two RBIs this series.
Anything else fans might want to know?
The Phillies are 1-3 in franchise history in win-or-go-home postseason games. They won Game 5 of the 1980 NLCS. They lost Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS, Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS and Game 5 of the 1981 NLDS.

item.title: [MLB.com] Red Sox turned away by Yanks in Wild Card Series for 2nd straight year
item.dc:creator: Ian Browne
item.description: NEW YORK -- Just when it looked like Willson Contreras had given the Red Sox some much-needed life with a solo homer to right-center with two outs in the sixth inning of Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees, the season essentially went up in flames in a disaster-filled bottom of the frame. The Statcast-projected 387-foot shot felt significant in the moment because it snapped a drought for the Red Sox of 26 postseason innings without a run dating back to Game 2 of la
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- Just when it looked like Willson Contreras had given the Red Sox some much-needed life with a solo homer to right-center with two outs in the sixth inning of Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees, the season essentially went up in flames in a disaster-filled bottom of the frame.
The Statcast-projected 387-foot shot felt significant in the moment because it snapped a drought for the Red Sox of 26 postseason innings without a run dating back to Game 2 of last year’s Wild Card Series (also against the Yankees).
But the Bronx Bombers made the short burst of momentum from Contreras feel insignificant when they erupted for six runs in a game-breaking, series-breaking bottom of the sixth inning that sent deafening roars throughout Yankee Stadium and the Red Sox to a 9-2 loss on Wednesday. Those reverberating sounds were a harsh reminder to the Red Sox that this was likely to be their last game of 2026.
With two flat performances in the final two nights of September, during which they were outscored, 18-2, the Red Sox were denied a chance to play in October. It also extended the streak to five straight seasons of no postseason baseball at Fenway Park.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there were quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series, and that ended for us tonight,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “So it's frustrating. And there's a lot of things you can say, but in the moment, right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it's going to take some time to get over that.”
It will go down as a roller-coaster spring, summer and brief autumn in Boston. There was the 32-46 hole, which the Sox somehow dug out of with a season-altering 32-5 stretch from June 25-Aug. 7 that included a franchise-tying winning streak of 15 games.
Then there was the final month of the regular season, which included injuries to key players and a stunning lack of offense, two themes that carried into the postseason.
“I'm proud of what we accomplished,” said veteran starter Sonny Gray, who took the loss. “Sour taste in your mouth for the ending. But we were left for dead there for a while, and I will definitely remember that run that we went on and what that felt like, because I've never experienced anything like that in my career -- to dig ourselves out of that hole and to put ourselves in this situation, that was a lot of fun.”
For the Red Sox, the fun ended in New York before it even started.
Quite simply, very little went right for the Sox in this two-game sweep at the hands of their rivals, which lacked the drama of last year’s set that went the distance (also won by the Yankees).
“For our season to end the same way that it did last year against our biggest rival, it sucks” said Red Sox lefty Garrett Crochet.
The bottom of the sixth served as a microcosm of the futility and frustration -- the inning that deep-sixed Tracy and his club.
With Contreras creating some energy in the Boston dugout, Tracy tried to add to it by bringing on Crochet for his first appearance in a game since April 25.
Crochet’s quest to get back in time for postseason play after left shoulder woes was a compelling storyline for the Red Sox, but one that didn’t work in real time.
The lefty seemed to get off to a solid start when he struck out Spencer Jones on a sweeper. But catcher Adley Rutschman’s block wasn’t a clean one, and he appeared to hesitate before throwing to first after retrieving the wild pitch. The initial call of out was overturned on replay. Jones then stole second and moved to third on Rutschman’s throwing error.
From there, things devolved. Crochet didn’t get an out and was charged with four runs, though only one of the three hits he allowed was well-struck.
“Personally, to think that I busted my [butt] the past five months, and for it to end that way, on a personal note, it's tough,” said Crochet. “I just wanted to come back and contribute to the team as best I could, and I let them down.”
Gray turned in a strong enough start for the Sox, giving up six hits over 4 2/3 innings and leaving with his team down 1-0.
But the offense never quite came around, and the bullpen had a second straight spotty night. And just like that, the season was over.
“Obviously disappointed,” said shortstop Trevor Story. “A lot of thoughts. Proud of this group, proud of this team. With all the [criticism] and everything around, the way this team came together, and really turned the season around to get back into this position is something that was special, and we're not going to forget that. Obviously, it's not about doing amazing things in the regular season. It’s about the postseason.”

item.dc:creator: FOX Wilmington
item.description: Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series was deadlocked at 3-3 Wednesday afternoon before Alec Bohm delivered Philadelphia’s biggest swing. His two-out homer in the 10th inning lifted the Phillies to a 4-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves and forced a winner-take-all Game 3. The Phillies had trailed 3-1 before Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers in the seventh. Harper’s blast came one inning after he committed a costly fielding error. item.content:encoded:
Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series was deadlocked at 3-3 Wednesday afternoon before Alec Bohm delivered Philadelphia’s biggest swing. His two-out homer in the 10th inning lifted the Phillies to a 4-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves and forced a winner-take-all Game 3.
The Phillies had trailed 3-1 before Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers in the seventh. Harper’s blast came one inning after he committed a costly fielding error.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
Andrew Painter then took over. The regular-season starter worked three scoreless innings to protect Philadelphia’s taxed bullpen, stranded two runners in the 10th and struck out Dominic Smith after the Phillies won an ABS challenge.
Playing under traditional extra-inning rules that don’t include designated runners at second base like in the regular season, Bohm delivered his third career postseason home run, a 357-foot shot to right field off right-hander Didier Fuentes.
The Phillies will try to continue their postseason dominance over the Braves in Thursday’s Game 3. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS.
In the seventh, Drake Baldwin’s double glanced off Harper’s glove in right field, driving in Sean Murphy to give Atlanta a 2-1 lead. Harper, who resumed playing the outfield late this season for the first time since 2022, got a poor jump and was leaping for the ball near the warning track. He was not charged with an error. Matt Olson added a sacrifice fly.
“Probably should have been caught, obviously,” Harper said.
The Phillies pulled even with eighth-inning home runs by Schwarber and Harper off Dylan Lee, the winning pitcher in the Braves‘ 5-3 opening win on Tuesday. Schwarber’s drive carried 447 feet and Harper followed with a 418-foot drive.
Tyler Mahle allowed one run on six hits in seven innings for Atlanta. Cristopher Sánchez allowed three runs in 6 2/3 innings for Philadelphia while throwing a career-high 116 pitches.

Tyler Mahle allowed one run on six hits in seven innings for Atlanta. Cristopher Sánchez allowed three runs in 6.2 innings for Philadelphia while throwing a career-high 116 pitches.
The start time for the decisive Game 3 has not yet been determined. The Braves announced that MLB will schedule the game for either 2:15 p.m. ET or 8:15 p.m. ET in Atlanta, with the final time dependent on the conclusion of the other three Wild Card Series Game 2 matchups tonight.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: [mlb.com] Houston? No problem! White Sox end 21-year wait with sweep
item.dc:creator: Scott Merkin

item.content:encoded:
HOUSTON -- There was a moment with nobody out in the sixth inning Wednesday night during Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series that perfectly encapsulated the White Sox remarkable season and the downright fun they’ve had along the way.
Chase Meidroth connected on a three-run home run off Bryan Abreu, turning a one-run lead into a 7-3 advantage, which was ultimately the final score. But it was Meidroth’s reaction that reinforced the point.
Meidroth pumped his fist and screamed with joy from the moment he connected until he touched home plate, his emotions on full display. Back in the visitors’ clubhouse, the champagne was chilling as the White Sox prepared to take another somewhat unexpected step in the postseason.
“When I’m locked in on the field, I don’t know what goes through my mind,” Meidroth said. “All I’m thinking about is me and the baseball and trying to compete. But I had a good feeling.”
Good feelings have surrounded the White Sox since Spring Training, even dating back to SoxFest in late January. They’ve arguably been baseball’s best story in 2026, and perhaps one of the best in sports.
But this two-game sweep against the undermanned Astros proved they are a talented team to be reckoned with throughout the postseason. They are more than the young, energetic squad that shook off three consecutive 100-plus-loss campaigns to reach the playoffs.
Their second clubhouse celebration in a week -- and one of five they hope to have this postseason -- marked their first playoff series victory since 2005. That last series victory was a four-game sweep over the Astros in the World Series, with Games 3 and 4 played at what is now Daikin Park.
“These players are scared of nothing,” White Sox general manager Chris Getz said. “And whether it be myself or others, it’s like, 'How do we continue to nurture and fuel this group?'”
"We were able to do that with two games that I thought were emblematic of how we've won all season,” manager Will Venable said. “Contributions from everywhere. Sammy [Antonacci] setting the tone, great job down the lineup with everyone behind him. Guys pitching in different spots, going out whenever and getting the job done, and they did it."
For the second straight game, Chicago took control in the first inning with the help of Houston's poor defense. The White Sox scored four runs off Astros ace Hunter Brown, who had a 6-0 record with a 2.39 ERA over six career starts against the White Sox entering Wednesday.
Antonacci doubled on a line drive to left field that Yordan Alvarez seemed to have a play on but didn’t make. Kyle Teel singled home Antonacci, and Miguel Vargas reached on third baseman Nick Allen’s fielding error.
Andrew Benintendi singled home a second run, and when Lucas Spence's throw home got away from catcher Yainer Diaz, Vargas scored the third run. Tristan Peters then added an RBI single to cap the scoring in the opening frame.
Houston crept back with solo home runs from Jeremy Peña, Cam Smith and Jose Altuve off White Sox ace Sean Burke, who struck out eight over four innings. The Astros had a golden opportunity in the fifth inning, putting runners on first and second with one out for Alvarez. Anthony Kay was on the mound for his first true relief appearance this season.
Kay fell behind in the count, 3-0, threw a pitch in the zone that was taken by Alvarez and then got him to fly out to Antonacci in left on the next pitch. Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases, but Altuve flied out to right to end the frame.
Then Meidroth provided breathing room in the sixth, launching his three-run homer to restore Chicago’s four-run lead. Twelve outs stood between the White Sox and playoff history, but they had reasserted control, and Erick Fedde handled the final two innings to finish it off.
“You saw how it was this series,” Kay said. “Everyone didn't worry about themselves, just played as a team and did the best they could.”
“Hard to imagine myself in that situation, honestly, but I'm so glad they chose me with the ball and to give the team the win,” Fedde said. “This whole fan base deserved [this]. This whole organization deserved [this]. Feels good to move on to the next round.”
And now, it’s on to Cleveland and the AL Division Series for the White Sox, in the ongoing saga between AL Central rivals. The White Sox won the season series, 7-6, but the Guardians won the division by one game to earn home-field advantage.
Cleveland features a strong rotation and one of the best closers in the game in Cade Smith. Then again, the Guardians will see a team on a roll that has been 21 years in the making.

item.title: [MLB.com] Bullpen stung by long ball after Mahle's strong playoff debut
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength. “I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength.
“I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.”
Nearly 40 years later, Weiss still remembers the sting he and his A’s teammates felt when an injured Gibson came off the bench to hit a walk-off homer against Hall of Fame closer Dennis Eckersley in Game 1 of the 1988 World Series at Dodger Stadium.
A similar type of sting was felt as the Braves blew a two-run eighth-inning lead in a 4-3, 10-inning loss to the Phillies in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Dylan Lee surrendered consecutive homers to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper in the eighth. Didier Fuentes allowed Alec Bohm’s decisive homer with two outs in the 10th.
“That's life,” Braves starting pitcher Tyler Mahle said. “Sometimes, it happens. There's nothing really else to say about it. It sucks now, but we're going to have a chance to go out there tomorrow and turn it around.”
Now, Weiss’ bunch must win Game 3 on Thursday to avoid being eliminated from the playoffs by Philadelphia for the fourth time overall and third time in the past five years. The Phillies eliminated Atlanta teams that won 100-plus regular-season games in 1993 (NLCS), 2022 (NLDS) and 2023 (NLDS).
Thursday's Game 3, airing on NBC and Peacock, will start at 8 p.m. ET.
“[The Braves] have played great at home,” Harper said. “But again, I'll just talk about the postseason; it's just a different animal.”
Mahle proved he was up to the challenge during what was his first postseason appearance. The right-hander, acquired from the Giants on Aug. 2, became the first Braves pitcher to allow one run or none over seven-plus innings in the postseason since Max Fried threw seven scoreless against the Reds in Game 1 of the 2020 NL Wild Card Series.
Once Harper misplayed a Drake Baldwin fly ball into a go-ahead double off Phillies starter Cristopher Sánchez during Atlanta’s two-run seventh, it looked like the Braves were destined for a great storyline.
But instead of celebrating how their trade acquisition helped them end the Phillies’ playoff dominance, the Braves were reminded that Lee hasn’t been nearly as good as he was before the All-Star break, when he posted a 1.47 ERA in 43 innings (44 appearances).
When Schwarber opened the eighth with a Statcast-projected 447-foot homer and Harper followed by depositing another ball into the right-field seats, Lee extended the troubles he had while posting a 6.00 ERA in 24 innings after the break. It should be noted he allowed just two homers during that stretch, and he did not allow any home runs to left-handed batters during the regular season.
“Lee’s our high-leverage lefty,” Weiss said. “He put down the same part of the order yesterday.”
Lee struck out Schwarber and got Harper to fly out in Game 1. How might he fare if he’s asked to go through these left-handed sluggers for a third straight day?
How about Fuentes? The rookie right-hander was masterful during the regular season, posting a 2.05 ERA in 70 1/3 innings as a reliever. But he surrendered J.T. Realmuto’s two-run triple in Game 1, and his psyche was bruised again Wednesday when Bohm sneaked his game-winning homer over the right-field wall.
“[Fuentes] made a good pitch,” Baldwin said. “I think if we need him tomorrow, he'll be ready to go, and I don't think he'll let that affect him too much.”
The Phillies’ rotation was a concern entering this series because Zack Wheeler was needed to pitch on Sunday with a postseason spot on the line. Well, Aaron Nola and Wheeler could be used in Game 3.
As for the Braves, they haven’t announced who will start Game 3. Grant Holmes will be lined up to pitch at least four innings. But will he start? Or will either Ray Kerr or Brent Suter take the mound as an opener?
More importantly, can the Braves bounce back from this and finally end their playoff struggles against their division rivals?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] PCA, Cubs meekly exit playoffs after offense disappears in 2-game Wild Card sweep by Padres

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO (AP) — The Chicago team that didn't have the pope on its side is heading meekly into the offseason.
Pete Crow-Armstrong and the Chicago Cubs came out to sunny San Diego and wilted like a tourist without enough sunscreen, swept out of the National League Wild Card Series by a San Diego Padres team eager for redemption and perhaps primed for a deep postseason run.
The Cubs lost 4-1 in Game 2 on Wednesday night at Petco Park to exit the postseason. They came in with the highest-scoring offense in the majors and head home having scored only one run on eight hits.
They were ushered out by the Reaper himself, San Diego's All-Star fireballing closer Mason Miller who allowed Nico Hoerner's one-out double — the Cubs' only extra-base hit in the two games — before getting Carson Kelly to ground out to shortstop to end it. The No. 4-seeded Padres move on to face the NL Central champion and top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers in an NL Division Series.
The loss by the fifth-seeded Cubs came several hours after the Chicago White Sox, who received a letter of support from lifelong fan Pope Leo XIV, swept the Houston Astros in Game two of an AL Wild Card Series.
The Cubs beat the Padres 2-1 in a Wild Card Series last fall at Wrigley Field.
Several Cubs players lingered along the dugout rail watching the Padres and their yellow towel-waving fans celebrate on a 69-degree night.
Players hugged inside the quiet clubhouse.
Crow-Armstrong, the frontrunner for NL MVP after becoming the first Cubs player to post a 40-40 season, struggled to find perspective while placing blame on himself.
"None of it feels good," Crow-Armstrong said. "That's it. So I'm just feeling pretty disappointed in myself, but that's for me to work on."
Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman, the Cubs' 1-2 hitters, combined to go 0 for 15 with one walk and eight strikeouts. Crow-Armstrong had the walk in Game 1. Each of them struck out three times in Game 1 while Crow-Armstrong had a walk.
Asked how he'd process his performance, Crow-Armstrong said: "That's not really for me to answer right now. I mean, yeah, you can look at the scoreboard, you can look at the stat sheet, wherever you get your numbers from, and it is clear to see that I didn't contribute. So, that's not for me to feel about right now. I wouldn't process that well if I was."
The Southern California native, who had 45 homers and 41 stolen bases, said the Cubs "showed a lot of heart and a lot of fight through all the challenge. But I mean, I would say to start, like, I show up. I show up when it matters in these games, you know? I think that would help us immediately, but that's all I got right now."
The Cubs dominated the season series 5-1. The teams hadn't seen each other since July 1, when the Cubs handed the Padres their worst loss ever, 23-3 at Wrigley Field as they hit eight home runs.
"The San Diego group, they threw the ball really well," Dansby Swanson said. "They didn't miss spots often, and if they did miss, it was in good locations. It's a really talented staff. They game-planned for us really well and we weren't able to get traction. We gave ourselves a couple of chances here and there, but, we weren't able to capitalize and keep anything going."
Said manager Craig Counsell: "You've just got to go play well and win games. In the end, we're walking away unfulfilled and disappointed."

item.title: [MLB.com] 'Never a doubt': Resilient Phils force Game 3 on three dramatic swings
item.dc:creator: Todd Zolecki
item.description: He removed his cap and sat in a crouch with two outs in the seventh inning on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly had just walked to the mound to remove Cristopher Sánchez from the game, two batters after Harper’s misplay on a fly ball to right sparked Atlanta’s go-ahead two-run rally in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series. Guns N’ Roses blasted throughout the ballpark as the Braves reveled in Harper’s misfortune. “Obviously a world of emotion there,” Harper
item.content:encoded:
He removed his cap and sat in a crouch with two outs in the seventh inning on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly had just walked to the mound to remove Cristopher Sánchez from the game, two batters after Harper’s misplay on a fly ball to right sparked Atlanta’s go-ahead two-run rally in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series. Guns N’ Roses blasted throughout the ballpark as the Braves reveled in Harper’s misfortune.
“Obviously a world of emotion there,” Harper said. “I'll tell you what. I was thinking about Krew, my son, what I would say to him in that situation.”
The Phillies were six outs from another crushing season-ending loss and perhaps significant offseason changes. But then the unbelievable happened. The Phillies won in 10 innings, 4-3. Kyle Schwarber and Harper hit back-to-back homers in the eighth inning to tie it. Alec Bohm hit an opposite-field homer in the 10th to take the lead. Rookie Andrew Painter pitched three scoreless innings of relief in the first postseason performance of his career.
“What a sport,” Harper said.
“A great gift,” said Jesús Luzardo, celebrating his 29th birthday.
“It’s in our DNA,” Schwarber said. “We’re just not going to quit.”
Thursday's Game 3, airing on NBC and Peacock, will start at 8 p.m. ET.
Sánchez allowed a leadoff walk in the seventh inning to Sean Murphy. Ha-Seong Kim bunted a ball toward the mound. Bohm, who turned a fantastic 3-2-3 double play to end the sixth, inexplicably tried to get the lead runner at second base. He did not.
Two batters later, Harper misjudged Drake Baldwin’s fly ball to right. It tipped over the top of his glove to allow a run to score.
Sánchez found Harper in the dugout afterward.
“I told him that he was bound to have a great moment,” Sánchez said via team interpreter Diego D’Aniello.
“I just tapped him on the butt and said, ‘You’ve got this,’” J.T. Realmuto said.
Schwarber started the inning against Braves left-hander Dylan Lee, who hadn’t allowed a homer to a left-hander in 92 at-bats this season. He hit a 3-2 slider a Statcast-projected 447 feet. Braves right fielder Ronald Acuña Jr. didn’t even bother to turn around to watch the ball leave the ballpark.
Harper greeted Schwarber at home plate.
“Hey, man, just try to find a way on,” Schwarber told Harper.
Instead, Harper smashed a 1-1 slider to right field to tie the game.
“I wasn't not trying to hit a homer, I can tell you that,” Harper said. “For me, everybody is going to make mistakes at some point, but it's how you come through in the next situation.
“It's not that serious, to tell you the truth. I think people take it very seriously -- and don't get me wrong, I take it serious. But I think there's a mindset, especially for kids nowadays, is parents and coaches put so much on kids these days to have to come through and be great. But for me, it's, 'How can you learn from each situation that you're in to come out great in the next one?'”
It was one of the more dramatic moments in Phillies postseason history considering how everything had unfolded in the bottom of the seventh inning, with the Phillies’ season and future of the organization on the line.
“What just happened,” reliever Tim Mayza said.
“That wasn’t stressful at all,” Zack Wheeler said.
Painter put up zeros to give the Phillies a chance to win it in the 10th.
“That’s a career-altering performance in my opinion,” Realmuto said.
Bohm hit the go-ahead homer in the 10th against Didier Fuentes.
“I didn't know it was gone until I heard it hit -- kind of rattle against the fence above the wall,” Bohm said.
It was Bohm’s first opposite-field home run since Opening Day. Bohm became the fourth player in Phillies history to hit a go-ahead homer in extra innings of a postseason game, joining George Vukovich (1981 NLDS Game 4), Lenny Dykstra (1993 NLDS Game 5) and Realmuto (2022 World Series Game 1).
“I've seen some great ones that this has happened to,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “I saw one of the greatest. I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers [Dennis Eckersley] of all time [in Game 1 of the 1988 World Series]. It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.”
But it’s not over yet. The Phillies need to win Thursday to keep their season alive. They are 1-3 in franchise history in win-or-go-home postseason games. They won Game 5 of the 1980 NLCS. They lost Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS, Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS and Game 5 of the 1981 NLDS.
“We have to keep going,” Schwarber said.
Painter struck out Dominic Smith looking on an 0-2 fastball -- after an appropriately dramatic and successful challenge by Realmuto, the first game-ending ABS challenge in postseason history -- to end the game at 5:19 p.m. ET. Trea Turner, who went 1-for-5 with a double, returned to the Phillies’ clubhouse by himself 32 minutes later.
He had just left the batting cage near the visitors’ dugout. He carried two bats in each hand.
He had been working, preparing for Game 3.
“Never a doubt,” Turner said about the win.

item.title: [MLB.com] Yanks sweep rival Sox behind another offensive onslaught to punch ticket to ALDS
item.dc:creator: Bryan Hoch
item.description: NEW YORK – This is only the first checkpoint of a postseason journey the Yankees hope will stretch deep into October. But if they had to choose an opponent to send home first, few would be more satisfying than the Red Sox. For the second consecutive year, that’s exactly what they did. Their celebration reflected that, with corks popped and bubbly spraying in every direction. Luis García Jr. hit an early homer and Cody Bellinger delivered a three-run dagger late as the Yankees trounced the Red So
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – This is only the first checkpoint of a postseason journey the Yankees hope will stretch deep into October. But if they had to choose an opponent to send home first, few would be more satisfying than the Red Sox.
For the second consecutive year, that’s exactly what they did. Their celebration reflected that, with corks popped and bubbly spraying in every direction.
Luis García Jr. hit an early homer and Cody Bellinger delivered a three-run dagger late as the Yankees trounced the Red Sox, 9-2, on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, sweeping the two-game American League Wild Card Series.
“Being able to celebrate with your teammates after a playoff series win, it doesn’t get old,” said left-hander Max Fried. “This is what we start practicing in February for. This is where we want to be. So it’s just about playing our game, having fun, and hopefully we’ve got a couple more of these we can do.”
The victory vaults the Yankees into the AL Division Series against the Rays, with Game 1 scheduled for Saturday at Tropicana Field. The Yankees plan to start either Gerrit Cole or Carlos Rodón, pitching coach Matt Blake said.
Following Schlittler’s lead, Fried permitted three hits over six innings of one-run ball, then leaned on the bats to do the rest against the Yankees’ most historic rival. This had been expected to be a low-scoring series, but New York made it lopsided.
“As I said all year, but even going into this series, that was a scary team to us – especially as well as they pitch,” manager Aaron Boone said. “I’m just really pleased with how we played. We’re going to enjoy that, and excited to get our shot at a really good Tampa [Bay] club.”
Imported to supply power with captain Aaron Judge on the injured list, García provided a big fourth-inning swing that represented an overwhelmingly left-handed lineup’s first dent against one-time Yankee Sonny Gray, who was touched for a pair of runs before exiting to a loud chorus of boos in the fifth.
Born in New York and counting himself as a Yankees fan before moving to the Dominican Republic in early childhood, García beamed as he crossed home plate, pointing into the crowd. He hit 30 home runs during the regular season, seven after being acquired from the Nationals in August.
“I only have one word – unbelievable,” García said. “You feel the crowd, you feel the fans. You feel everything right now. This experience for me, it’s unbelievable.”
Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay, then delivered a run-scoring single to greet left-hander Erik Miller in the fifth – the second time in as many nights Miller surrendered a run to the first batter he faced, having allowed Ben Rice’s first of two homers in Game 1.
The Yankees broke it open with a six-run sixth, sending 10 batters to the plate. Rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. collected his first postseason RBI, setting up Austin Wells and Ryan McMahon to knock in runs.
“This shows what we can do,” Lombard said. “We’re obviously a great clubhouse, a great group of guys. When everything’s going our way, when we’ve got all our guys competing like we are now, I think we can do a lot of great things.”
Bellinger capped the rally, slugging a Garrett Whitlock changeup into the seats. This time, Boston intentionally walked Rice to face Bellinger. It didn’t work.
“I was very surprised they were willing to face Cody Bellinger, a guy who absolutely thrives with runners in scoring position and has done it his whole career,” Rice said. “Interesting decision.”
Said Bellinger: “That was a cool moment. I feel like I was able to enjoy that one. Home game in Yankee Stadium, it’s a really fun atmosphere. It’s fun to play, and hopefully we get many, many more this month.”
Willson Contreras and Nick Sogard homered for the Red Sox, who went 26 innings without scoring a postseason run before Contreras’ sixth-inning shot off Fried – a streak that dated back to Game 2 of last year’s AL Wild Card Series in the Bronx.
Given that drought, the Yanks’ firepower was too much to overcome.
“You’re thinking we're going to play closer games,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “They swung the bats extremely well. You've got to give them credit. It was frustrating.”
Now the Yankees turn their attention to the Rays, who claimed the division by 4 1/2 games during the regular season and won seven of 13 meetings with New York this year.
But October can change everything, and right now, the Yankees are confident they will.
“I know we didn’t win the division,” said Judge, who is hoping to be activated for the next round. “We weren’t the No. 1 seed, got put in the Wild Card. But we’re not trying to make a statement. We’re trying to play our game and take care of business.”

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong went hitless again Wednesday as the Cubs were eliminated by the Padres.

Crow-Armstrong did draw a walk in Game 1, but he went 0-for-7 with four strikeouts as the Cubs’ leadoff hitter in the series. Alex Bregman went 0-for-8 in the two hole behind him. Crow-Armstrong also didn’t help matters tonight by wasting a challenge during the very first at-bat of the game. It’s definitely not how he was looking forward to completing his MVP campaign. However, through 10 career postseason games, he’s 5-for-34 with no extra-base hits and a 16/2 K/BB ratio.

item.title: [newstribune.com] White Sox sweep Astros for first postseason series win since 2005 | Jefferson City News-Tribune
item.dc:creator: MK Bower; Field Level Media
item.description: HOUSTON -- Chase Meidroth hit a backbreaking three-run home run in the sixth inning to help the Chicago White Sox make a big early lead stand up in a 7-3 victory Wednesday against the Houston Astros that capped a two-game sweep of their American League wild-card series. The White Sox earned their first postseason series victory since their sweep of the Astros in the 2005 World Series. The White Sox will face the Cleveland Guardians in a best-of-5 American League Division Series that begins Satur
item.content:encoded:
HOUSTON -- Chase Meidroth hit a backbreaking three-run home run in the sixth inning to help the Chicago White Sox make a big early lead stand up in a 7-3 victory Wednesday against the Houston Astros that capped a two-game sweep of their American League wild-card series.
The White Sox earned their first postseason series victory since their sweep of the Astros in the 2005 World Series. The White Sox will face the Cleveland Guardians in a best-of-5 American League Division Series that begins Saturday in Cleveland.
“I’m really just happy for everybody over the last few years who experienced White Sox baseball when it obviously wasn’t at its best,” Chicago manager Will Venable said postgame. “It’s such a storied franchise. (White Sox owner) Jerry (Reinsdorf) put so much into this team, loves this team so much, and to be able to reward him and the city of Chicago, who have been in our corner and supported us from Day 1 that I’ve been there, just feels really good.
“I’m proud of the guys and certainly happy for them. They’re probably the only ones in this country that believed they could be in this spot, and they maintained that belief in the beginning of the season and went throughout the season maintaining that. They made it happen.”
The Astros returned to the playoffs after a one-year absence but have not advanced past the wild-card round since 2023.
“(Astros owner) Jim (Crane) has been very clear about his process and when he wants to have that conversation,” Houston manager Joe Espada, who finishes the season without an extension in place to stay with the Astros. “I respect the process and how blessed I’ve been to have been here for over nine years, experienced so many division titles, championship series, World Series -- winning one as a bench coach. As a manager, I have witnessed so many great moments. Obviously, I would like to continue enjoying those moments.”
After the Astros left the bases loaded in the fifth, Meidroth extended a 4-3 lead by driving a 3-1 slider from Astros reliever Bryan Abreu 390 feet to left-center field.
The White Sox scored four runs in the top of the first inning off Astros ace Hunter Brown (0-1), who didn’t make it out of the first as he allowed five hits, four runs (three earned) and one walk while the defense contributed two errors.
Kyle Teel, Andrew Benintendi and Tristan Peters recorded RBI singles in the first while Miguel Vargas reached on a fielding error by Astros third baseman Nick Allen and scored on a throwing error by center fielder Lucas Spence. Brown retired two of the nine batters he faced.
The Astros began a methodical climb back into the game in the bottom of the first when leadoff man Jeremy Pena smacked the first of three solo home runs off Chicago starter Sean Burke.
Pena drilled a 1-1 slider 395 feet to left-center field. An inning later, Cam Smith bashed a 1-0 sinker 440 feet to left field to close the margin to 4-2. In the fourth inning, Jose Altuve socked his 28th career postseason homer -- second all-time to Manny Ramirez -- to left to bring Houston within 4-3.
Burke allowed three runs and four hits while recording eight strikeouts in four innings. When the Astros built another serious threat in the fifth, White Sox left-hander Anthony Kay delivered.
After reliever Huascar Brazoban hit Cam Smith with a pitch and gave up a single to Pena, Kay (1-0) entered with one out and retired MVP candidate Yordan Alvarez on a deep fly just in front of the Crawford Boxes in left. Kay loaded the bases by walking Isaac Paredes but induced Altuve into a harmless flyout to right to end the inning.
Peter Lambert, the Astros’ third pitcher of the game, needed only 36 pitches to work three perfect innings, but he walked Benintendi and Peters to open the sixth. After Abreu entered the game, Meidroth faked a bunt that enabled pinch runner Luisangel Acuna and Peters to steal third and second base, respectively. With the infield in, Meidroth made it moot by crushing a hanging slider he immediately knew was a home run.

item.title: [CubsHQ] Everything Dansby Swanson said before Game 2 against Padres
item.dc:creator: Tony Crumpton
item.description: Dansby Swanson addressed the media at Petco Park ahead of Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series to discuss the Chicago Cubs' mindset following a Game 1 loss. Watch the video below: Q. item.content:encoded:
Dansby Swanson addressed the media at Petco Park ahead of Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series to discuss the Chicago Cubs' mindset following a Game 1 loss.
Watch the video below:
Q. You guys have talked all season long about this team's ability to kind of reset and start anew each new day. Are you seeing that so far today, and how do you think that's going to be able to benefit you guys today?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think we've all -- this whole year we've had opportunities to respond to adversity, and this is obviously no different. We have such a professional group, a group that prides itself on getting better each and every day no matter the circumstance. So business as usual in that regard.
Q. What is it like knowing you guys have Gausman starting tonight, given his experience in big playoff moments like this and just seeing his track record?
DANSBY SWANSON: He's pitched in a lot of big games in his career, in his life. We were thrilled to be able to acquire him at the deadline just knowing that experience and what he brings, the toughness, the pitch ability, and being able to have him on our team to help navigate through moments like this is a big part of why he's here.
He's been so good for us all year in big moments, and I expect nothing different tonight.
Q. From your experience, what's the key in games like today?
DANSBY SWANSON: Really and truly, it's just about being locked in on every pitch, just laying it all out there and understanding that we're at our best when we do what we do best.
At this time of year, it can be challenging because you go so in depth with the other team and trying to navigate what they're going to do, what we're going to do. I think the greatest reminder is, if we do what we do best, then we feel like we're a really good baseball team.
Q. Yesterday Craig went with Pedro at third. Today he goes with Matt Shaw. You saw what Pedro did when you were out. Just what's it like knowing those are the two guys you have behind the main group when something happens with Bregman or happened with you or somebody else?
DANSBY SWANSON: The depth of this group has definitely been a strength, a guy who's able to play multiple positions, able to put together great at-bats off different types of pitchers, and really just the personality piece. Great guys in the clubhouse and the ability to just add to our roster in terms of whether it's hitting left-handed pitching, right-handed pitching, being able to play second base, third base, slide around wherever is needed.
Without them, I doubt that we're in a position that we're in right now. So thankful for those guys, thankful for what they bring every day. Very glad that they're on our team.
Q. We've asked Bregman questions like every day since that day in Cincinnati, and he came back so quickly. Can you just put it into context, like what he's done and kind of what he's playing through and how kind of crazy it is when you take a step back and see what's happened over the past ten days or so?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think, if anyone knows Breggy, some facial fractures weren't going to stop him. He's dedicated to this game. He's dedicated to his craft. He's dedicated to his teammates, trying to find ways each and every day to not only personally get better, but to be able to help guys on the team get better.
It's been so fun being able to be on a team with him, just seeing what he does every day and what he brings to a group. I expect nothing else out of him at this point, doing whatever he can to be able to go out there, take the field. He knows that we're better when he's out there.
Q. Obviously you didn't really get much game action coming back from your injury. Just how have you been feeling with where your swing is at and just your comfort level in the box?
DANSBY SWANSON: Obviously baseball is a game that's meant to be played every day. When you miss a significant amount of time, it presents its own challenges coming back into it. I think kind of somewhat accepting that and going through the rehab process and understanding the position I was going to need to be in in order to get back to be as good as I can be was something that did drive me during that timeout.
It's like unfortunately, but also fortunately, having that time to be able to just kind of reflect and be able to do whatever I can to get back on the field and help this team win baseball games.
That's what I feel is a strength of mine as part of this group, and so thankful to be part of a group that is willing to step up in each and every way and not to overly say that I have to be the one to get things done or whatever. We're a group, we're a team, and we continue to push forward in that way.
Q. What's it been like to see Pete do what he's done this year with the idea that he's still so early in his career and he's got so much more to learn from and use to get better over the years?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think one of the really impressive things about Pete is the thing we've always seen, the physical ability, just the tools that he has, the strength, the defense, the base running. But to be able to really slow the game down this year and understand what he's trying to do at the plate to be able to -- I don't know if we've seen as significant of like a change in like walk rate or swing rate and all those kinds of things as we have with him.
He's just gotten so good at knowing what he's trying to do, how he's trying to execute, and been really stubborn at sticking to that. I think that's one of the big reasons why you've seen his game go into a new level is the ability to like mentally process things much quicker than it was earlier in his career. I think obviously that will only continue to get better.
To be able to do that at such a young age with more or less the different pressures you may have on you and attention on you, he's handled it so gracefully. It's been really, really cool to watch. Obviously having been somewhat in his shoes before and then being on like the older side, the veteran side of things, it's really cool to see him go through that and handle things the way he does.
Q. Obviously you guys have one of the best defenses in baseball, MVP candidate having a crazy, great season, and one of the best offenses. How important is it to take advantage of a season like this when you have the opportunity in the playoffs?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think each year is its own year, right? I think we don't really pay too much attention to those kinds of things. I think this group knows what it's capable of, so it's always reaching for the highest of heights that it can. That's one thing that I do love about this group is the relentless pursuit of really greatness together.
That's something that we've done all year. It's been kind of like a consistent mentality of ours all year. That's why it's so fun to be in positions like this because this is -- you know, being in situations like this is something that can only add to that confidence and to that mentality.
Q. Maybe a dumb question, but you guys from a distance obviously have a phenomenal defense. You've got great defensive players. That's got to be a huge part of it. Do you feel like this team maybe the last couple years compared to other teams you've been on puts an extra emphasis on that at all or goes out of the way to take advantage of the fact that you have the kind of defensive talent you do?
DANSBY SWANSON: It's almost like the last of a dying breed, right? Just like defense, no matter how great we've been offensively and the things we've done on the base pass, defense really is kind of our calling card.
It's interesting because it's not like something I would say that we like go above and beyond to work on it more. Jed and company have put together a great defensive roster obviously because we understand that defense really can change games. When you have Gold Glove-caliber defenders all over the yard, it makes it really tough on teams.
We understand that going out there and doing our part makes it hard for people to score on us. It's really fun to be a part of something like that. Give a lot of credit to the front office for being able to put together a team that is capable of doing more things than just playing defense, but it's wild when you go from really great defenses to not great defenses and like how much it can change things. We've been so consistent at remaining true to ourselves all year.
Q. Yesterday Gausman was saying that you treat this game like any other game except there's all those yellow towels flying around, and it can feel like momentum in these games in the postseason can feel even more real. What's it like managing that side of the game and the postseason?
DANSBY SWANSON: The biggest thing is accepting that it is the same game, right? It's the same rules other than the extra innings if there's not somebody on second base. But it's the same rules.
And being able to embrace that we are prepared and we've just got to go leave it all out there each and every day, each and every pitch, every inning and understanding that things can turn it one swing of the bat, one play in the field, one pitch, and just consistently attacking each and every pitch, whether it's on offense or defense.
Q. The pitching staff has obviously been through a lot this season. Can you just describe what it's been like watching how Counsell, the staff have pieced it together, especially at this point in the season and in a game like this where obviously it's all hands on deck?
DANSBY SWANSON: It's kind of wild when you like kind of ride it out, just the injuries that we've sustained, the things that we've gone through in the pitching department itself. Give a lot of credit to the guys that are here now, obviously Tommy and the rest of the pitching staff for being able to consistently find ways to improve the group and get guys better.
Then you look at just some of the acquisitions and all those kinds of things and really being able to identify traits that are going to play well at this time of year. It's really impressive what Counsell is able to do really putting each guy in a great position to succeed. It sounds simple, but he does it at a really, really high rate. I think it's something that he's really, really good at.
He's done well for the pitching staff, and they've obviously rewarded him in the same way by throwing the ball well. Very thankful for that and the hard work that everyone's done to be able to get to this point. Hopefully we'll go out there and put together a complete performance tonight.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] AL Wild Card Series Game 2: Max Fried vs. Sonny Gray
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Nielsen
item.description: In the words of a Yankee legend, it was dèja vu all over again in the Bronx last night as Cam Schlittler continued crafting a legend of his own. Just like last season, Schlittler delivered a gem of a performance against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, staking New York to a 1-0 series lead and giving them an opportunity to close the affair out early tonight. But unlike last year's three-game set, in which the Yankee offense never fully erupted, the lineup finally achieved escape velocity. Be
item.content:encoded:
In the words of a Yankee legend, it was dèja vu all over again in the Bronx last night as Cam Schlittler continued crafting a legend of his own. Just like last season, Schlittler delivered a gem of a performance against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, staking New York to a 1-0 series lead and giving them an opportunity to close the affair out early tonight. But unlike last year's three-game set, in which the Yankee offense never fully erupted, the lineup finally achieved escape velocity. Ben Rice and his four hits, two homers, and six RBI, led the charge — but the bottom of the lineup contributed their fair share as well.
In other words, the Yankees played the perfect ballgame last night. Max Fried will be tasked with carrying the momentum into Game 2. Fried's second season in pinstripes has been marred by a couple of IL stints limiting him to just 20 starts and 112.2 innings, but when he's been healthy, he's been just as good as in 2025. He'll be pitching on seven days' rest in Game 2 — his last appearance was an up-and-down start against the Rays, in which Tampa clinched the AL East.
As far as the recent track record against Boston, Fried has been quite effective. He only faced them twice this season: one was a short start from when he was returning from his latest injury, the other an eight-inning masterpiece in April from before the Red Sox got it together under new manager Chad Tracy. In Game 1 of last year's WCS, he provided 6.1 scoreless innings, scattering four hits three walks while striking out six. The Yankees couldn't hold onto the narrow 1-0 lead he had defended, and sabotaged their own comeback effort after loading the bases with nobody out in the ninth inning. None of that was Max's fault, of course. Provided the lineup supports him, an effort like last year's will be more than enough.
Old friend Sonny Gray never caught on with the Yankees in 2017 and 2018, but he'll have no choice but to step up under the Yankee Stadium lights with Boston's season on the line. Over his first season with the Red Sox, the steady veteran turned in yet another outstanding season, leading the AL with 18 wins (don't think that doesn't mean anything to him) and pitching to a 2.72 ERA. That's the thing about the Red Sox' pitching: they have lots of exciting youngsters like Payton Tolle, who pitched last night, but they also routinely get the most out of their veteran pitchers too. Gray faced New York twice in June and pitched well both times. The latter outing was his best start of the season by game score — one hit, one walk, nine strikeouts over 7.1 scoreless innings.
Unsurprisingly, Aaron Boone's lineup for Game 2 is nearly unrecognizable when compared with the Game 1 starting nine. It's a history-making card: according to James Smyth of the YES Network, it's the first time a team has put eight lefty batters — switch hitters not included — in the same lineup in the postseason. The portside octet includes Trent Grisham, who entered late last night for his first action off the IL. Rice will ascend to the leadoff spot, with Cody Bellinger and Luis Garcia Jr. to follow. Spencer Jones hits cleanup and plays right field ahead of George Lombard Jr., the lone righty to get the start. Jazz Chisholm Jr. draws in at the keystone, Grisham bats in the seven-spot after him, Austin Wells will bat eighth, and Ryan McMahon starts at third and will hit ninth. Naturally, expect plenty of right-handed bats to come off the bench against a lefty-heavy Boston staff once Gray's start concludes.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Yankees make MLB history with lefty-loaded lineup for Wild Card Game 2 vs. Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Peter Sblendorio
item.description: The Yankees made MLB playoff history in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, starting eight true left-handed hitters to face right-handed Boston Red Sox starter Sonny Gray. Never before had a team started that many lefty batters — not including switch-hitters — in a postseason game, per the Elias Sports Bureau. “I saw our lineup and I assumed that was probably the case,” one of those lefties, Cody Bellinger, told the Daily News with a grin. “I didn’t know. We’ve got a lot of talent in this locker roo
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees made MLB playoff history in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, starting eight true left-handed hitters to face right-handed Boston Red Sox starter Sonny Gray.
Never before had a team started that many lefty batters — not including switch-hitters — in a postseason game, per the Elias Sports Bureau.
“I saw our lineup and I assumed that was probably the case,” one of those lefties, Cody Bellinger, told the Daily News with a grin. “I didn’t know. We’ve got a lot of talent in this locker room.”
It was in stark contrast to Tuesday night’s Game 1, when the Yankees started only four left-handed batters against Red Sox lefty Payton Tolle in an eventual 9-0 win in the Bronx.
On Wednesday night, lefty-swinging first baseman Luis García Jr., second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., center fielder Trent Grisham and third baseman Ryan McMahon all returned to the starting lineup as the Yankees sought platoon advantages.
Lefty-hitting Spencer Jones, who started Game 1 in center field, moved to right field for Game 2.
Meanwhile, righty-swinging Paul Goldschmidt, Heliot Ramos, Amed Rosario and Anthony Volpe all began Wednesday’s game on the bench after starting Game 1.
Rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. was the only right-handed batter in Wednesday’s lineup.
Gray is actually a bit tougher against lefty batters than righties, but because the Red Sox carry five left-handed relievers, Boone said he liked having a bench full of right-handed batters that he could deploy in the later innings.
The best-of-three Wild Card Series allows for this kind of maneuvering because, given its short nature, teams are able to carry more hitters and be more aggressive with their bench moves.
The Yankees carried 16 position players in the Wild Card Series, compared to just 10 pitchers.
That likely won’t be the case in future rounds, when they would need to use a fourth starting pitcher and cover more innings with their bullpen.
But Games 1 and 2 against the Red Sox showed how the Yankees plan to approach the postseason, with matchups dictating their lineup decisions perhaps more than they have in the past.
“With this group, I feel like it’s going to take everyone,” manager Aaron Boone said Wednesday. “So that’s my plan — day in and day out, it’s going to be a little different, potentially. And that phrase ‘all hands on deck’ certainly applies to us with our team right now.”
The Yankees need to prioritize lineup creativity even more because the matchup-proof Aaron Judge is sidelined indefinitely with a calf strain.
Giancarlo Stanton — who also typically starts against righties and lefties — is currently relegated to pinch-hitting duty after missing more than five months due to three separate calf strains.
And Wednesday marked the first game started by Grisham since Sept. 4, when he suffered a hamstring strain. After being activated for the Wild Card round, Grisham entered Game 1 in the seventh inning as a defensive replacement and went 0-for-1 at the plate.
“I know he’s ready to go,” Boone said. “I liked his at-bat [in Game 1] when he came in, hit a ball well to center. I don’t know what I’m going to get from any of the guys tonight. But I’ve got a lot of confidence in who he is and what he can bring to the table.”
The Yankees became even more platoon-oriented after they acquired García and Ramos, both of whom perform to traditional splits, before the Aug. 3 trade deadline.
All of those factors led to Wednesday’s historic, lefty-loaded lineup.
“It’s super beneficial for us, because all the guys in the lineup are super tight — righties and lefties — and there will be a lot of different conversations between different guys in what they saw, how they picked it up,” Jones told The News.
“And then we’ve got a bunch of guys ready to go off the bench.”
SCHMIDT SHUT DOWN
Clarke Schmidt’s season is officially over.
The right-hander has been shut down after landing on the IL with right biceps neuritis shortly after making his long-awaited return from Tommy John surgery.
Boone said last week that it was his understanding Schmidt would be shut down, but he hadn’t confirmed it until Wednesday.
But Boone said Schmidt is doing “fine.” That’s in line with what Boone shared last week, when he said Schmidt was expected to have a normal winter to build up for spring training.
More than a year after undergoing elbow surgery, Schmidt made his season debut on Sept. 16 and recorded two outs in a relief appearance.
A starter by trade, Schmidt had hoped to help out of the Yankees’ bullpen this postseason.
But Schmidt experienced a cramping sensation as he warmed up for a second relief appearance, then returned to the IL last Thursday.
VOLPE NEWS
Volpe has a new agent, confirming to The News that he is now being represented by Scott Boras and the Boras Corporation.
Boras is baseball’s most prolific agent, representing stars such as Juan Soto, Gerrit Cole and Bellinger.
Volpe, 25, is eligible for free agency after the 2028 season.

Sonny Gray is set to take the mound for the Red Sox in a crucial game, bringing his array of five to six well-executed pitches that effectively keep hitters off balance. Despite Gray not being a high strikeout pitcher, his skillset suggests another low-scoring game could be on the horizon.

item.content:encoded:
Pat Murphy provided an update on Joey Ortiz as the Milwaukee Brewers prepare for their National League Division Series opener.
Ortiz underwent an MRI over the weekend, with Murphy saying the structural results were good. However, the Brewers manager remains cautious because Ortiz is dealing with a bruised right knee and abdominal swelling.
Ortiz has not played since leaving Milwaukee's Sept. 25 game against the St. Louis Cardinals in the eighth inning.
Brewers Manager Pat Murphy said Andrew Vaughn is a full go this week, but they are still keeping an eye on Joey Ortiz’s abdomen and knee.
Murphy says Ortiz will be a “little limited” and they are keeping him from some of the higher intensity activities in today’s workout.
The Brewers have extra time to monitor Ortiz because their 103-59 regular season earned them a first-round bye. Milwaukee will open the NLDS on Oct. 3 against the winner of the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres Wild Card Series.
Ortiz was an important part of the Brewers' infield during the regular season. He appeared in 134 games and hit .270 with a .328 on-base percentage, .402 slugging percentage, nine home runs, 47 RBI and nine stolen bases.
Ortiz also recorded 100 hits, 14 doubles and four triples while drawing 35 walks. His availability could give Milwaukee another option in the infield as the team begins its postseason run.
For now, Murphy is giving Ortiz time rather than rushing him back into game action. The seven-day window between his last regular-season appearance and the NLDS gives the Brewers additional time to evaluate his condition.
Milwaukee enters October after winning 103 games, but Ortiz's health is one of the situations the team will continue monitoring before Game 1. His status should become clearer as the Brewers get closer to their postseason opener.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Bryce Harper saves Phillies' season with massive home run vs. Braves after ugly misplay earlier in game
item.dc:creator: Mike Axisa
item.description: The duality of Bryce Harper was on full display Wednesday afternoon in Atlanta. In the span of six batters in the seventh inning, Harper badly misplayed a ball in right field that allowed the go-ahead run to cross the plate and hit a game-tying home run as part of back-to-back homers with Kyle Schwarber. Harper also drove in the game's first run with a single in the first inning. He went 2 for 5 in the Phillies' Game 2 win (PHI 4, ATL 3 in 10 innings). "Schwarb, Harp, after we give up those two,
item.content:encoded:
The duality of Bryce Harper was on full display Wednesday afternoon in Atlanta.
In the span of six batters in the seventh inning, Harper badly misplayed a ball in right field that allowed the go-ahead run to cross the plate and hit a game-tying home run as part of back-to-back homers with Kyle Schwarber. Harper also drove in the game's first run with a single in the first inning. He went 2 for 5 in the Phillies' Game 2 win (PHI 4, ATL 3 in 10 innings).
"Schwarb, Harp, after we give up those two, they got momentum," Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. "And to be able to get that back right away was huge."
Philadelphia rearranged its defense to accommodate Luis Arraez at the trade deadline, which pushed Alec Bohm from third base to first base and Harper from first base back to right field. The results were not always positive. On Wednesday, Bohm failed to get an out on a bunt in that seventh inning immediately prior to Harper's misplay. Drake Baldwin lifted a fly ball that Harper misplayed into a double, which gave the Phillies a 2-1 lead.
"Obviously a world of emotion there," Harper said of his misplay. "I didn't think he hit it very hard and I realized he only hit 89 (mph exit velocity), so I thought it was going to be a pop fly just right at me and then it kind of kept traveling. Obviously a ball I should have caught."
Based on the exit velocity and launch angle, Statcast registered Baldwin's double -- "double" -- with an .080 expected batting average. Stats aside, it's a ball that must be caught, much like Ha-Seong Kim's bunt was a ball that had to be turned into an out. Bohm hesitated just enough for Sean Murphy to beat the throw to second base. Little things that cost the Phillies.
"I think it's a ball Bryce probably thinks he should have caught," Mattingly said. "It looked like it kept carrying a little bit. But no, you don't need to say anything to guys like that in that spot, not in this moment."
Matt Olson followed Baldwin's double -- again, "double" -- with a sacrifice fly to give the Braves a 3-1 lead in the seventh inning. The two misplays contributed directly to the two runs. Harper redeemed himself, though. He and Schwarber hit the back-to-back homers in the next half-inning to tie the game 3-3.
Those were the first two home runs Braves setup man Dylan Lee gave up to left-handed batters this season.
"Lee is our high-leverage lefty," Braves manager Walt Weiss said. "Put down the same part of the order yesterday pretty easily. Threw the ball really well yesterday. That's his inning every time."
Bohm redeemed himself as well. After botching the bunt, he hit a go-ahead home run in the top of the tenth inning, which stood up as the game-winning run thanks to Andrew Painter's heroic three-inning relief appearance. The Phillies have pulled even with the Braves in the Wild Card Series. The decisive Game 3 will be played Thursday afternoon.
"There's been a lot of ups and downs," Bohm said about his season. "Didn't start the best. I don't really know how to put it all into words quickly, but it's just been a long road with a lot of ups and downs. I've learned a lot, and I've made a lot of really close friends along the way and had a lot of people to lean on along the way. I really wouldn't have rather had it any other way."
To make the infield work with Arraez, the Phillies shifted Bryson Stott from second base to third, Bohm from third base to first, and Harper from first base to right. Prior to Arraez's arrival, Harper had not played the outfield since 2022. He moved to first base that summer to limit his throwing following his return from Tommy John surgery.
Arraez rolled his ankle at the end of the regular season and is not on the Wild Card Series roster. His status for the rest of the postseason, should the Phillies advance, is up in the air.

item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball announced today that it has approved a roster substitution for the Boston Red Sox due to an injury sustained by outfielder Roman Anthony. As a result, Anthony will be replaced by Curtis Mead on Boston’s roster vs. New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series presented by AbbVie. Dr. Gary Green, MLB’s Medical Director, confirmed the injury after a full review of the medical information.
MLB Postseason rules provide that a Club may request permission from the Commissioner’s Office to replace a player who is unable to play because of an injury. The Commissioner’s Office may approve or disapprove the request based on the specific facts and circumstances. In accordance with the rules, Anthony will be ineligible to return in the American League Division Series presented by Booking.com if the Red Sox participate, but he would be eligible to return for the American League Championship Series if Boston qualifies.
The Wild Card Series presented by AbbVie will be broadcast by NBC, Peacock and NBC Sports Network while ESPN Radio provides live national coverage. MLB Network will air extensive studio coverage throughout the Postseason across the Emmy Award-winning MLB Tonight, the Emmy-nominated MLB Central and MLB Now, and Intentional Talk, MLB Network’s longest-running talk show. Postseason games throughout 2026 will also be telecast in Spanish on Universo and Univision, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. The 2026 Postseason will be distributed by MLB media rightsholders in 16 different languages to fans in more than 200 countries and territories.
